name: Low
label: Sub Pop
lede: A married Mormon couple from Duluth played as quietly as they could in the loudest years of grunge, and for almost thirty years made the smallest sounds in rock feel enormous, until Mimi Parker's death ended the band.

eras.title: Quiet in the grunge years
eras.text: Alan Sparhawk and Mimi Parker had known each other since grade school in Clearbrook, Minnesota. In Duluth they started a band built on a dare: what happens if you play this slow and this soft when everyone else is playing loud?

years.h: Low's first two shows at RecyclaBell in Duluth
years.p: Alan Sparhawk and Mimi Parker, both members of the LDS Church, recruit bassist John Nichols. Parker plays one snare, one cymbal and one floor tom, almost always with brushes.
years.xp: Sparhawk had played in Zen Identity across the bridge in Superior, Wisconsin. He's described the idea as half joke, half experiment: what would Duluth crowds do with music this quiet while grunge was the loudest thing going. The band never liked the word slowcore.

years.h: I Could Live in Hope with Kramer, on a Virgin imprint
years.p: The debut is produced by [[Kramer|d898e082-70d1-4a86-ac8e-ecdf89892994]] and released on Vernon Yard, a Virgin Records imprint. John Nichols plays bass.

years.h: Long Division: Zak Sally replaces John Nichols
years.p: Bassist Zak Sally joins for the second album, starting a ten-year run in the band.

years.h: The Curtain Hits the Cast and a college radio hit
years.p: "Over the Ocean" gets real play on college radio and the band becomes a critics' favorite.

eras.title: Kranky, Albini and a Gap ad
eras.text: Moving to Chicago's Kranky, Low made two records with Steve Albini that many fans still rank as their best, and a slow Christmas song ended up selling khakis on network TV.

years.h: Low records Secret Name with Steve Albini
years.p: Nine days at [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]]'s Electrical Audio in Chicago produce the first Low album for Kranky. Zak Sally adds Optigan to some songs.

years.h: Secret Name, Low's first album on Kranky
years.p: Released by Kranky with Tugboat in the UK. The Washington Post said Low had done something new without losing its serenity.

years.src: Wikipedia: Things We Lost in the Fire
years.h: Things We Lost in the Fire, the second Steve Albini record
years.p: Opening with "Sunflower" and closing with the instrumental "In Metal," it scores 87 on Metacritic. The Guardian's 2019 critics' poll ranks it 93rd of the century so far.
years.xp: Pitchfork put it at 117 on its list of the best albums of the 2000s. Low played the whole record at a Don't Look Back show in 2006. Argentine writer Mariana Enriquez, a fan, named her story collection after it.

years.h: Trust, mixed at Peter Gabriel's Real World
years.p: The last Low album on Kranky is recorded by Tom Herbers and Eric Swanson, then mixed by Tchad Blake at Real World Studios.

years.h: Low's "Little Drummer Boy" soundtracks a Gap snowball fight
years.p: Gap uses Low's hymn-slow cover of "The Little Drummer Boy" in a slow-motion snowball-fight ad. A remix of Low's "Halflight" turns up in The Mothman Prophecies.

years.h: Zak Sally quits Low, then stays
years.p: Zak Sally leaves briefly. The band posts that everyone had to work through personal things, and that the good news is Zak is remaining.

years.h: Low tours Europe with Radiohead
years.p: Low opens for [[Radiohead|a74b1b7f-71a5-4011-9441-d0b5e4122711]] across Europe with Zak Sally back on bass.

eras.title: Louder, and a breakdown in public
eras.text: Signing to Sub Pop, Low made its loudest record yet and started charting in the US. Then Alan Sparhawk cancelled a tour and told fans why.

years.h: Low signs to Sub Pop and boxes up ten years of rarities
years.p: Low joins Sub Pop, and its own Chairkickers' Union label releases A Lifetime of Temporary Relief: 10 Years of B-Sides and Rarities.

years.h: The Great Destroyer with Dave Fridmann
years.p: The first Sub Pop album, produced by Dave Fridmann, has what the Village Voice called comparatively thunderous verve. It's Low's first to chart in the US.

years.big: The tour stops. Alan Sparhawk says why.
years.h: Alan Sparhawk cancels The Great Destroyer tour over depression
years.p: Sparhawk calls off the second leg and publishes a statement about his struggle with depression. In August he's back, touring with [[Mark Kozelek|99f4b23d-3711-4efe-ad71-9572158e234c]].

years.h: Zak Sally leaves; Matt Livingston brings a Navy pump organ
years.p: After ten years Zak Sally quits. Matt Livingston takes bass and saxophone and plays an antique Navy chaplain's pump organ.

years.h: Drums and Guns, Matt Livingston's only album
years.p: Livingston plays on the record and leaves afterwards.

years.h: Steve Garrington joins on bass and keys
years.p: Steve Garrington starts a twelve-year stint, playing on four studio albums.

eras.title: Robert Plant, Swans and a 27-minute protest
eras.text: Low's songs started showing up in other people's hands, from Robert Plant to Swans. Onstage they were still willing to baffle a festival crowd on purpose.

years.h: Robert Plant covers two Low songs on Band of Joy
years.p: Robert Plant records "Monkey" and "Silver Rider" from The Great Destroyer, and says Low's music played in his house next to Jerry Lee Lewis and Howlin' Wolf.

years.h: C'mon, Steve Garrington's first Low album
years.p: Low's ninth studio album, and the first of four with Garrington on bass.

years.h: Alan Sparhawk and Mimi Parker sing on Swans' "Lunacy"
years.p: The pair add vocals to the opening track of [[Swans|3285dc48-9505-469d-ad8a-bdf2d3dba632]]' The Seer.

years.h: 27 minutes of one song at Rock the Garden
years.p: At Minneapolis's Rock the Garden, Low plays one slowed-down "Do You Know How to Waltz?" for its whole set, and the crowd and internet split over it.
years.xp: Alan Sparhawk ended it with a line borrowed from an anti-drone activist's sticker. The Invisible Way came out the same year.

years.h: Ones and Sixes on Sub Pop
years.p: The band's eleventh album.

years.h: Double Negative, the most radical turn of Low's career
years.p: Garrington's last album with Low, and the first of two records that bury Sparhawk and Parker's voices in electronic distortion.

eras.title: Low is and was Mimi
eras.text: Mimi Parker was diagnosed with ovarian cancer and Low kept working, as a duo, until it couldn't. Her death on November 5, 2022 ended the band.

years.h: Mimi Parker diagnosed with ovarian cancer; Low becomes a duo
years.p: Parker is diagnosed late in 2020 and starts treatment in 2021. Steve Garrington has left, so Low is officially Alan Sparhawk and Mimi Parker alone.

years.h: Hey What, the last Low album
years.p: Released on Sub Pop. Liz Draper, bassist for Charlie Parr, is hired to play the songs live.

years.h: Mimi Parker reveals her cancer on a podcast
years.p: Parker makes her diagnosis public in a podcast interview. Through the year Low cancels European dates and Death Cab for Cutie support shows for her treatment.

years.h: Low's last show: Water Is Life Festival, Duluth
years.p: Low's final performance is at home in Duluth.

years.h: Mimi Parker dies of ovarian cancer at 55
years.p: Parker dies surrounded by family. The band's message asks fans to keep her name close and sacred and to share the moment with someone who needs them.

eras.title: After Low
eras.text: Alan Sparhawk confirmed Low was over and kept making music, first with his son in a new band, then under his own name, while Robert Plant kept Low songs in his sets.

years.h: Alan Sparhawk's new band Damien, with son Cyrus on bass
years.p: Formed in late 2021 with singer Marc Gartman and drummer Owen Mahon, Damien releases The Boy Who Drew Cats.

q: Low is and was Mimi. It was amazing. I'm grateful.
years.h: Alan Sparhawk confirms Low ended with Mimi Parker
years.p: On Twitter, Sparhawk says Low was and is Mimi, and that he's grateful for all of it.

years.h: Alan Sparhawk's solo album White Roses, My God
years.p: Sparhawk's second solo record, followed in May 2025 by an album with Trampled by Turtles.

years.h: Robert Plant leads his new album with a Low cover
years.p: "Everybody's Song" is the first single from Plant's Saving Grace, fifteen years after he first covered Low.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Things We Lost in the Fire
